messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
The standard deviation (standard error) of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis is  

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx 0.22 .
\]

So the null‑hypothesis test has a standard deviation of roughly **0.22**.

They likely want the standard error of the mean difference? Actually standard deviation of the null hypothesis test: maybe they want the standard error of the sample mean under null: sigma/sqrt(n). But we have sample std dev 1.4, sample size 40. So standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2215. But they mention population mean 98.6. That might be used for t-statistic: (98.2 - 98.6)/SE = -0.4/0.2215 ≈ -1.805. But question: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" maybe they want the standard error? But we don't know population sigma; we use sample sigma as estimate: 1.4. So SE = 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 0.2215. So answer: about 0.2215.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test statistic: t = (sample_mean - population_mean)/(sample_std_dev/sqrt(sample_size)). The denominator is SE. So the standard deviation of t distribution is sqrt(df/(df-2))? Actually t distribution has variance df/(df-2) for df>2. For df=39, variance = 39/(39-2)=39/37≈1.054. Standard deviation ≈ sqrt(1.054)=1.026. But that's not what they ask.

Might be ambiguous. But likely they want the standard error of the mean difference: sqrt((sample_std_dev^2)/sample_size). So answer: 0.2215.
